L174: cite84†Vladimir Yugay*†vladimiryugay.github.io · cite85†Kersten Thies*†scholar.google.com · cite86†Luca Carlone†lucacarlone.mit.edu · cite87†Theo Gevers†staff.fnwi.uva.nl · cite88†Martin Oswald†oswaldm.github.io · cite89†Lukas Schmid†schmluk.github.io L175: 
L176: ### cite90†Project Page†vladimiryugay.github.io L177: ## ⚙️ Setting Things Up
L178: 
L179: Clone the repo:
L180: 
L181:     `git clone https://github.com/VladimirYugay/GaME.git
L182:     `
L183: 
L184: We tested the installation with `gcc` and `g++` of versions 10, 11 and 12. Also, make sure that `nvcc --version` matches `nvidia-smi` version.
L185: 
L186: Run the following commands to set up the environment
L187: 
L188:     `conda create -n game python=3.10 -y
L189:     conda activate game
L190:     `
L191: Install pytorch:
L192: 
L193:     `# CUDA 11.8
L194:     conda install pytorch==2.5.1 torchvision==0.20.1 pytorch-cuda=11.8 -c pytorch -c nvidia
L195:     # CUDA 12.1
L196:     conda install pytorch==2.5.1 torchvision==0.20.1 pytorch-cuda=12.1 -c pytorch -c nvidia
L197:     # CUDA 12.4
L198:     conda install pytorch==2.5.1 torchvision==0.20.1 pytorch-cuda=12.4 -c pytorch -c nvidia
L199:     `
L200: Install other dependencies:
L201: 
L202:     `conda install -c conda-forge faiss-gpu=1.8.0 git-lfs
L203:     pip install ./submodules/diff-gaussian-rasterization/ --no-build-isolation
L204:     pip install ./submodules/flashsplat-rasterization/ --no-build-isolation
L205:     pip install ./submodules/simple-knn/ --no-build-isolation
L206:     pip install -r requirements.txt
L207:     `
L208: ## 🔨 Running GaME
L209: 
L210: Here we elaborate on how to load the necessary data, configure GaME for your use-case, debug it, and how to reproduce the results mentioned in the paper.
L211: 
L212: Getting the Data We tested our code on Flat and Aria datasets. Make sure to install git lfs and hugging face cli before proceeding.
L213: Flat was created by cite91†Panoptic Mapping authors. However, it is a bit tricky to find it on the web. Therefore, we uploaded it to HF datasets for easier access. Install git lfs and download it by running:
L214: `git lfs install`
L215: `git clone cite92†https://huggingface.co/datasets/voviktyl/GaME_Flat†huggingface.co `
L216: Aria consists of clips from cite93†AriaDigitalTwin†www.projectaria.com . The clips are covering the area that undergoes changes outside of the camera view. You can download already processed data with the command:
L217: `git clone cite94†https://huggingface.co/datasets/voviktyl/GaME_Aria†huggingface.co `
L218: 
L219: Running the code
L220: 
L221:     `python run.py --config_path configs/<dataset_name>/<config_name> --data_path <path_to_the_scene> --output_path <output_path>
L222:     `
L223: For example:
L224: 
L225:     `python run.py --config_path configs/AriaMultiagent/room0.yaml --data_path <path_to>/AriaMultiagent/room0 --output_path output/AriaMultiagent/room0
L226:     `
L227: 
L228: Check the configs to set up wandb for loggin.
L229: 
L230: Reproducing Results While we tried to make all parts of our code deterministic, differential rasterizer of Gaussian Splatting is not. The metrics can be slightly different from run to run.
L231: If you are running on a SLURM cluster, you can reproduce the results for all the datasets by running the files in the `scripts` folder. For example, for Aria dataset:
L232: 
L233:     `./scripts/reproduce_aria_sbatch.sh
L234:     `

L178: # MoPe: Motion Permanence for Robust Monocular Gaussian Mapping in Dynamic Environments
L179: 
L180: Qixin Xiao
L181: 
L182: University of Michigan, Ann Arbor
L183: MoPe extends monocular Gaussian SLAM with a memory-aware temporal posterior that accumulates dynamic evidence across frames, guides tracking and mapping with that posterior, and performs Gaussian-level post-cleanup to suppress persistent ghosting in dynamic scenes. It realizes Motion Permanence: the principle that an object's dynamic identity should persist over time rather than be re-decided from each frame independently.
L184: ## Overview
L185: 
L186: Monocular Gaussian SLAM works well in many scenes, but dynamic distractors remain a major failure mode. A single-frame uncertainty estimate is fundamentally memoryless: once a moving object slows down, pauses, or reappears after occlusion, the current frame can look static again and dynamic content may leak into the map.
L187: 
L188: MoPe addresses this limitation with a temporal evidence pipeline that:
L189:   1. propagates a posterior of dynamic evidence across time with SE(3)-consistent warping,
L190:   2. fuses the propagated prior with current-frame uncertainty and semantic cues in log-odds space,
L191:   3. reuses the resulting temporal posterior during pose tracking, memory-aware mapping, and Gaussian insertion,
L192:   4. performs Gaussian-level post-cleanup through evidence collection and opacity decay.
L193: The current repository contains the MoPe configurations used in our experiments, together with scripts for benchmark reproduction and artifact-focused analysis on `iphone_wandering`.
L194: ## Repository Highlights
L195: 
L196:   * `src/utils/dyn_uncertainty/temporal_fusion.py`: temporal posterior propagation and fusion utilities.
L197:   * `src/depth_video.py`: posterior-guided tracking and person-prior integration.
L198:   * `src/mapper.py`: memory-aware mapping, insertion masks, and Gaussian-level cleanup.
L199:   * `scripts_run/`: single-sequence and batch benchmark runners for Wild-SLAM MoCap.
L200: ## Installation
L201: 
L202: Clone the repository with submodules:
L203: 
L204:     git clone --recursive https://github.com/chloeqxq/TEG-SLAM.git
L205:     cd TEG-SLAM
L206: 
L207: Create the environment. The helper scripts default to the environment name `wildgs-slam`.
L208: 
L209:     conda create --name wildgs-slam python=3.10
L210:     conda activate wildgs-slam
L211: Install CUDA 11.8 and the core PyTorch stack:
L212: 
L213:     pip install numpy==1.26.3
L214:     conda install --channel "nvidia/label/cuda-11.8.0" cuda-toolkit
L215:     pip install torch==2.1.0 torchvision==0.16.0 torchaudio==2.1.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu118
L216:     pip install torch-scatter -f https://pytorch-geometric.com/whl/torch-2.1.0+cu118.html
L217:     pip install -U xformers==0.0.22.post7+cu118 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu118
L218: Pin `setuptools` before editable installs:
L219: 
L220:     pip install setuptools==78.1.1
L221: 
L222: Install the local CUDA extensions and project dependencies:
L223: 
L224:     python -m pip install -e thirdparty/lietorch/
L225:     python -m pip install -e thirdparty/diff-gaussian-rasterization-w-pose/
L226:     python -m pip install -e thirdparty/simple-knn/
L227:     python -m pip install -e .
L228:     python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
L229: Install `mmcv-full` for the metric depth estimator:
L230: 
L231:     pip install mmcv-full -f https://download.openmmlab.com/mmcv/dist/cu118/torch2.1.0/index.html
L232: 
L233: Download the pretrained DROID-SLAM weights and place them in `pretrained/droid.pth`:
L234: 
L235:     mkdir -p pretrained
L236:     # Download:
L237:     # https://drive.google.com/file/d/1PpqVt1H4maBa_GbPJp4NwxRsd9jk-elh/view?usp=sharing
L238: Verify the installation:
L239: 
L240:     python -c "import torch; import lietorch; import simple_knn; import diff_gaussian_rasterization; print(torch.cuda.is_available())"
L241: ## Quick Start
L242: 
L243: ### 1. Crowd demo on Wild-SLAM MoCap
L244: 
L245: Download the demo sequence:
L246: 
L247:     bash scripts_downloading/download_demo_data.sh
L248: 
L249: Run MoPe on the `crowd` sequence:
L250: 
L251:     bash scripts_run/run_wild_slam_mocap_v6_sequence.sh crowd --profile report
L252: 
L253: This wrapper will:
L254: 
L255:   * generate a temporary benchmark config with temporal posterior, person-aware insertion gating, and Gaussian-level cleanup enabled,
L256:   * run SLAM,
L257:   * evaluate NVS automatically,
L258:   * save outputs under `output/`.
L259: ### 2. Real-world `iphone_wandering` stress test
L260: 
L261: Download the Wild-SLAM iPhone dataset:
L262: 
L263:     bash scripts_downloading/download_wild_slam_iphone.sh
L264: 
L265: Run the MoPe config:
L266: 
L267:     python run.py ./configs/Custom/wandering_temporal_proposal_v6.yaml
L268: 
L269: This setup is the artifact-focused real-world case used in the report to study persistent human ghosting and post-cleanup behavior.
L270: If you hit CUDA out-of-memory, reduce the rendering resolution in the selected config, for example:
L271: 
L272:     cam:
L273:       H_out: 240
L274:       W_out: 400
L275: ## Reproducing the Report
L276: ### Wild-SLAM MoCap benchmark
L277: 
L278: Download the full 10 dynamic sequences:
L279: 
L280:     bash scripts_downloading/download_wild_slam_mocap_scene1.sh
L281:     bash scripts_downloading/download_wild_slam_mocap_scene2.sh
L282: 
L283: Run all benchmark sequences and build the aggregated report package:
L284: 
L285:     bash scripts_run/run_wild_slam_mocap_v6_all.sh --profile report
L286: 
L287: Useful options:
L288:   * `--skip-existing`: reuse finished sequence outputs.
L289:   * `--skip-report`: run the SLAM jobs without rebuilding the final summary package.
L290:   * `--max-frames N`: smoke-test a shortened run.
L291:   * `--profile conservative`: use the more conservative temporal thresholds.
L292: 
L293: Important outputs:
L294: 
L295:   * per-sequence SLAM and NVS results under `output/`
L296:   * aggregated report package under `output/`
L297: ### Single-sequence reproduction
L298: 
L299: To run one sequence only:
L300: 
L301:     bash scripts_run/run_wild_slam_mocap_v6_sequence.sh person --profile report
L302: 
L303: Supported sequence keys are:
L304: 
L305:     `anymal1 anymal2 ball crowd person racket stones table1 table2 umbrella
L306:     `
L307: ## Key Temporal Parameters
L308: 
L309: The report-ready configs enable the following controls under `mapping.uncertainty_params.temporal_params`:
L310: Parameter  | Role
L311: --- | ---
L312: `tracking_use_temporal_posterior`  | Uses the propagated posterior in tracking-time BA weighting.
L313: `mapping_use_temporal_posterior`  | Reuses the temporal posterior during mapping-time uncertainty filtering.
L314: `fusion_mode: log_odds`  | Fuses propagated and current dynamic evidence in Bayesian-style log-odds space.
L315: `person_prior_activate`  | Adds a semantic person prior to strengthen dynamic detection for people.
L316: `insertion_mask_activate`  | Prevents likely dynamic regions from inserting new Gaussians.
L317: `post_cleanup_opacity_decay_activate`  | Applies Gaussian-level evidence collection and opacity decay after the run.
L318: Useful starting configs and templates live in `configs/Custom/`, including:
L319: 
L320:   * `configs/Custom/custom_template.yaml`
L321: ## Running on Your Own Data
L322: 
L323: Organize RGB frames as:
L324: 
L325:     `your_sequence/
L326:       rgb/
L327:         frame_00000.png
L328:         frame_00001.png
L329:         ...
L330:     `
L331: 
L332: Then:
L333: 
L334:   1. copy `configs/Custom/custom_template.yaml`,
L335:   2. set `scene`, `data.input_folder`, and camera intrinsics,
L336:   3. enable or tune the temporal parameters if you want the full MoPe behavior,
L337:   4. run:
L338: 
L339:     python run.py /path/to/your_config.yaml
L340: ## Outputs and Evaluation
L341: 
L342: After a run, the most useful files are:
L343: 
L344:   * `traj/metrics_full_traj.txt`: full-trajectory ATE summary when ground-truth poses are available.
L345:   * `traj/est_poses_full.txt`: estimated camera poses in TUM format.
L346:   * `nvs/final_result.json`: novel view synthesis metrics for Wild-SLAM MoCap sequences.
L347:   * `gaussian_insertion_stats.json`: insertion-mask statistics for MoPe runs.
L348:   * `post_cleanup_stats.json`: Gaussian-level cleanup statistics.
L349: You can also summarize trajectory metrics with:
L350: 
L351:     python scripts_run/summarize_pose_eval.py

L353:

L229: Sparse-view regularization. Without regularization, ball_bounce and ball_roll degrade by $+3.0$ and $+4.2$ dB respectively on evaluation cameras, confirming that regularization is essential when training views are clustered.
L230: ## 5 Discussion and Future Work
L231: When does physics help? The advantage of physics over kinematic baselines scales with both occlusion duration and contact complexity. On ball_fall (248 frames, ground bounce during occlusion), physics outperforms even the non-causal linear interpolation by $+3.78$ dB, while on ball_roll (45 frames, nearly linear segment), kinematic models are competitive.
L232: The noise tolerance ablation reveals a smooth, monotonic relationship between trajectory accuracy and reconstruction quality (${\sim}1$ dB per $\sigma{=}0.25$), indicating that even approximate physics estimates are preferable to kinematic assumptions when contacts are present.
L233: This suggests a practical decision criterion: physics priors are most valuable when the occluded interval contains contact events that produce nonlinear trajectory changes, and least necessary when the trajectory is approximately ballistic.
L234: Parameter observability. Parameter identifiability depends on which physical interactions the cameras can observe. On ball_bounce, where first ground contact occurs during occlusion, friction is unobservable from pre-contact visible frames regardless of loss function. The curriculum addresses this by matching each parameter to the frames where it is identifiable.
L235: Preliminary two-pass experiments, where post-occlusion observations refine the physics parameters, show up to $+0.80$ dB improvement on ball_bounce by enabling friction estimation from re-emergence frames, suggesting that iterative refinement is a promising direction.
L236: More broadly, the identifiability analysis reveals a fundamental tension: the scenes where physics helps most (complex contacts during occlusion) are precisely those where the relevant parameters are hardest to estimate from visible frames alone.
L237: Causality and practical applicability. Linear interpolation, despite competitive performance on two scenes, requires the re-emergence position, which is unavailable in any causal or predictive setting. Against constant velocity, the only causal baseline, physics provides a consistent $+2.46$ dB advantage, making PersistGS the strongest causal method evaluated.
L238: This causal property is essential for downstream applications such as robotic planning and digital twin maintenance, where an agent must reason about occluded object locations in real time without access to future observations. The decomposed architecture (static background plus per-object SE(3)) further supports such applications by providing an explicit object-level representation that can interface directly with a planner or controller.
L239: Architecture. The decomposed architecture proved essential: a joint 4DGS baseline [cite27†32 ] overfits by $+6.9$ dB with only 5 training cameras, confirming that the sparse-view setting demands separation of static and dynamic components.
L240: This finding aligns with concurrent work on decomposed dynamic Gaussian representations [cite38†14 , cite40†42 ] and suggests that physics-based trajectory supervision is most naturally integrated within object-centric architectures where each rigid body has an explicit SE(3) trajectory to constrain.
L241: Limitations and future work. Spherical objects provide a clean validation of the translational component of our centroid silhouette loss, since sphere silhouettes are rotation-invariant. For asymmetric objects, the silhouette covariance (second central moment of the alpha map) captures projected orientation and offers a natural extension to jointly constrain translation and rotation without relying on appearance.
L242: The full SE(3) pipeline, including rotation-aware SH evaluation, is implemented and exercised during reconstruction. Validating on objects where orientation produces distinct visual changes is a natural next step. Extending to multi-object scenes with inter-object contact, and integrating automatic decomposition methods [cite37†38 ] to remove the requirement for known object segmentation, are further directions.
L243: ## 6 Conclusion
L244: We presented PersistGS, a method that uses differentiable rigid body simulation as a physics prior for 4D Gaussian Splatting, maintaining object permanence through temporal occlusion. By estimating friction and velocity from visible frames via a centroid silhouette loss and observability-aware curriculum, and positioning object Gaussians along the resulting SE(3) trajectory, PersistGS produces faithful reconstructions through observation gaps.
L245: On three scenes with contact events during occlusion, it outperforms constant velocity extrapolation by $+2.46$ dB PSNR and comes within $0.19$ dB of the ground-truth upper bound. The centroid loss yields 40% lower trajectory error than photometric supervision, and modifications to Newton’s contact kernels enable effective gradient flow through rigid body dynamics.
L246: These results establish analytical physics simulation as a principled alternative to generative priors for 4D reconstruction from temporally incomplete observations.
